title: Wrong options only knowledge can reject
statement: Each wrong option must attract a student who misunderstood, and only the tested knowledge or the text may rule it out, never common sense or surface cues.
example: With the rule and a scoring fix, a question whose wrong options were giveaways went from passing at 0.9143 to failing about 80% of runs.
detail: An AP evaluator's rubric fails a question when a wrong option can be ruled out by general reasoning, test-taking instinct or surface cues without the content the item assesses, which turns it into a logic puzzle; it names absolutes that carry the claim, self-contradiction with the stem, claims false on their face and options off the stem's named topic, and a guard catches the right answer being the only option that repeats a distinctive word from the stem. Before the fix, a question whose wrong options were all implausible or giveaways still passed at ~0.91, because one zeroed score was averaged away; after it, the reproducer went from PASS@0.9143 to failing ~80% of runs, with distractor_quality=0.0 in 23-25/30. No wrong option may be rejectable by common sense, a sweeping absolute, a contradiction of the stem or of another option, being true of any text on the topic, or lying outside the question's topic, period or category, and none may be generic filler. Each wrong option should also attract a student who misunderstood.
against: Keyed to surface words the rule over-fired: the model treated any absolute word as a giveaway and failed sound items, so it was narrowed to absolutes that carry the claim, and the rubric now warns that an option that is merely incorrect is not a giveaway. The code guard for negations fires only when every key follows the stem's direction and every wrong option opposes it (`icloud-work/inceptbench-main/src/inceptbench/evaluators/guards.py`, lines 962-974). The shares are among leaked items only; no rate for clean items is given (`grade3-reading/artifacts/alpha-read-packager/generator/g5/GENERATOR_REPAIR_KIT.md`, lines 13-15). A review accepted obviously wrong options in an end-of-lesson fill-in: "For blank 3, `charged`/`marched` "into the night" are grammatical but clearly wrong, which is acceptable." (`shadow-content-eval/reports/G3-U1-L14-review.md`, line 100). The training report's claim that fill-in passes at twice the multiple-choice rate does not match its own table, which gives 30.7% against 23.2% and 17.9% (`icloud-work/incept/ML_TRAINING_INSIGHTS_REPORT.md`, lines 293-295 and 430). A first attempt at same-theme wrong options for one item regressed to 1 of 3 and was reverted, reason not given, and the report warns that such options must not become defensible alternate keys. The two misses were stopped by the solver's own scope check, not by a grader verdict: "causing local rejection and then live IB timeout" (icloud-work/aptraining/workspace/comms/from_den/2026-05-22T2050Z_DELIVERED_pipeline_solver_v7_supersedes_v6.md, line 51). A word-usage check may rightly test one register violation with every wrong option, and one review downgraded the same-misuse finding to minor for that reason (`grade3-reading/artifacts/peter-pan-standing-2026-09-11/readiness-l5-2026-09-17/sim-review/agent-B-D5-D6-D11-D13.md`, line 21).

- **Topically misaligned distractors**: When a question stem has a clear topical focus (e.g., asks for evidence of "economic impact" or "political structure"), distractors that address entirely different topics from the stem's named focus are poor distractors. Students can eliminate them by topical mismatch alone without subject knowledge.
Students can identify the answer through simple keyword matching rather than subject knowledge.

Narrow the rule with a removal-check: the absolute is a giveaway only when the universality is *load-bearing* (deleting the absolute word leaves no plausible claim, or the absolute contradicts the stem's own premise).

**Near-neighbour distractors.** Distractors are built from *real passage details*, with … the wrong actor / stage / effect / cause / claim swapped in. No distractor may be absurd … or eliminable by world knowledge alone. (Absurd distractors leak the key by elimination.) … At G5, a near-neighbour distractor should require *returning to a specific sentence to … reject* — that is the bar.

**Bait the blind solver.** When a world-knowledge default exists, make it a *wrong* … option (a "live trap"). This actively *punishes* the non-reader rather than merely failing … to help them. At G5, the most common GK default is the textbook-true generalization; if … the passage takes a specific or counter-typical stance, key to the passage and make the … textbook generalization a distractor.
